10x10.h2: 10x10 ft, a finished consulting room in miniature
10x10.intro: The smallest floor in our premium office line, and the one professionals pick when a single room has to impress: a consulting desk, tinted glazing, LED panels set in a false ceiling and SPC flooring underfoot. Everything a visitor touches or sees has been specified on the drawing rather than defaulted at the factory. Clinics, advocates and property marketing suites take this size for one-to-one meetings where the room itself does part of the persuading. The premium sits in the surfaces, so even the smallest body carries the full finish schedule.
10x10.imageAlt: Full side view of the modern office cabin, 10 x 10 ft, a wide glazing band set into the clean panel face across the 10 ft wall.

20x8.h2: 20x8 ft, the slim premium office for street frontage
20x8.intro: A narrow premium body for showroom forecourts and street-facing plots where the office is also the signage. The long wall takes the tinted glazing run, so the interior reads from outside, and two desk positions sit behind it in a finished shell of laminate and LED. Dealerships and rental desks use exactly this arrangement. Where the ordinary slim cabin hides beside a gate, this one is placed to be seen, and the finish schedule is what makes that front-of-plot placement earn its keep commercially.
20x8.imageAlt: Complete exterior of the modern office cabin, 20 x 8 ft, the tall window opening breaking the wall run along the 20 ft flank.

20x10.h2: 20x10 ft, the benchmark size in its premium form
20x10.intro: The most-ordered footprint in India, delivered here with the upgraded schedule: larger tinted windows, premium laminate walls, LED lighting in a finished ceiling and SPC or LVT floor. Four people work in a room that reads like leased commercial space rather than a site placement. Companies choose this size when the cabin is the office their clients visit, not the one behind the hoarding. Same structure as the standard build, so the premium you pay is visible in the room rather than hidden in the frame.
20x10.imageAlt: The whole modern office cabin, 20 x 10 ft, a wide glazing band set into the clean panel face over the 20 ft length.

20x12.h2: 20x12 ft, finished width for a proper meeting table
20x12.intro: The extra width takes a real meeting table in a finished setting: six chairs, tinted glass beside them, LED panels above. In the standard line this floor hosts a working corner; in the premium line it hosts a client presentation. Sales offices for plotted developments and builder floors are the classic buyers, because the deal is closed inside the cabin itself. The laminate and flooring schedule continues under the table, which is exactly the detail where cheaper meeting rooms quietly give themselves away.
20x12.imageAlt: Wide exterior view of the modern office cabin, 20 x 12 ft, the tall window opening breaking the wall run on the 12 ft end wall.

30x10.h2: 30x10 ft, a premium front room with a working back
30x10.intro: The partition line earns its keep differently here: the front two-thirds is the finished client zone with glazing, LED and premium surfaces, while the rear third works as records, pantry or staff space behind a flush door. One delivered body gives a reception-grade room and a private working area. Sales galleries and admission offices run precisely this split. The finish schedule concentrates where visitors stand, which keeps the premium spend purposeful instead of spreading it thin across shelving and storage.
30x10.imageAlt: Overall view of the modern office cabin, 30 x 10 ft, the tall window opening breaking the wall run down the 30 ft side.

40x8.h2: 40x8 ft, a finished ribbon of glass along a frontage
40x8.intro: Forty feet of premium frontage on a strip plot: the glazing run turns the whole long wall into display, and the interior carries the finish schedule from end to end. Showrooms for tiles, sanitaryware and building products use this shape as a walk-through gallery with desks at one end. It is the only size in the premium line bought as much for what every passer-by sees as for the people who sit inside it, and the tinted run is what separates it from the plain slim cabin doing quiet duty at a site gate somewhere.
40x8.imageAlt: Long exterior view of the modern office cabin, 40 x 8 ft, a wide glazing band set into the clean panel face along the full 40 ft run.

40x10.h2: 40x10 ft, a branch office you do not have to build
40x10.intro: Reception at the door, open desks in the middle, a glazed manager cabin at the end: the layout of a leased branch office, delivered as one finished body. Eight to ten staff work in premium surroundings from the day of placement. Finance, insurance and real-estate branches on plots without built space are the regular buyers. Every zone carries the same laminate, lighting and floor specification, so the room reads as one designed space rather than a site cabin that happens to have one good corner.
40x10.imageAlt: Side-on view of the modern office cabin, 40 x 10 ft, the tall window opening breaking the wall run across the 40 ft elevation.

20x20.h2: 20x20 ft, the finished square for open teams
20x20.intro: Two matched halves joining into a four-hundred-square-foot square, finished to the premium schedule across the seam: continuous flooring, matched laminate, mirrored lighting. Open teams sit in clusters with a briefing space at the centre, and the tinted glazing keeps the room bright without heat. Design studios and marketing teams working from site take the square for the same reason they would in leased space, because collaboration needs width before anything else, and here the width arrives already finished.
20x20.imageAlt: Full-length view of the modern office cabin, 20 x 20 ft, a wide glazing band set into the clean panel face around the 20 ft square plan.

40x12.h2: 40x12 ft, the largest floor in our premium line
40x12.intro: The full 480 square feet carrying the complete finish schedule: cabins, meeting room and open desks planned on your drawing, all glazed, lit and floored to the premium standard. Twelve or more staff run a genuine head-office outpost from it. Developers running long sales programmes and companies posting managed teams to site take this floor when the alternative is a commercial lease. It is the largest single body in the premium line, and its rate per square foot is the lowest anywhere in the premium line.
40x12.imageAlt: Full elevation of the modern office cabin, 40 x 12 ft, a wide glazing band set into the clean panel face over the 40 by 12 ft body.

prefabricated-office-cabins.h2: Prefabricated Office Cabin sizes for multi-unit orders
prefabricated-office-cabins.guidanceLine: Tier pricing applies from three units on one purchase order, single or multiple destinations.

10x10.h2: 10x10 ft, the repeatable gate unit across sites
10x10.intro: Ordered in threes and fives rather than one at a time: identical gate offices for every entrance of a campus, or one per site across a district rollout. Because each unit is fabricated to the same drawing, the fifth arrives indistinguishable from the first, which is the entire point for an operations team standardising its estate. Facility companies and infrastructure contractors put this size on rate contract and call units off as sites open. One drawing approval at the start covers every placement that follows it.
10x10.imageAlt: Full side view of the prefabricated office cabin, 10 x 10 ft, bolted panel modules meeting on a visible grid across the 10 ft wall.

20x8.h2: 20x8 ft, the slim unit ordered by the corridor
20x8.intro: Metro corridors, pipeline stretches and road packages need the same slim office repeated every few kilometres, and this is that unit: a narrow body fabricated in batches, delivered in sequence as work fronts open. Procurement buys the batch once, and the drawing, the electrical set and the price hold across every delivery. Package contractors who have fought inconsistent one-off cabins across a long alignment order it precisely to stop that variation for good, unit after unit after identical unit.
20x8.imageAlt: Complete exterior of the prefabricated office cabin, 20 x 8 ft, module lines running vertically through the wall face along the 20 ft flank.

20x10.h2: 20x10 ft, the standard multi-site office, by the batch
20x10.intro: The reference office bought the procurement way: three, five or ten identical two-hundred-square-foot units on a single order, each matching the approved drawing to the millimetre. Site teams get a familiar office at every posting; head office gets one invoice, one specification and one warranty position across the fleet. This is the size most multi-site programmes standardise on, and the tier price at three units and again at higher counts is what separates this page from ordering one cabin three times.
20x10.imageAlt: The whole prefabricated office cabin, 20 x 10 ft, bolted panel modules meeting on a visible grid over the 20 ft length.

20x12.h2: 20x12 ft, the wider standard for programme offices
20x12.intro: Programmes that hold weekly reviews at every site standardise on the wider body, because the weekly meeting corner needs to exist at every location, not only at the flagship site. Ordered as a set, every location gets the same room in the same layout, so a visiting programme manager walks into a fully familiar office in every single city. The two extra feet cost the same modest step at every unit in the batch, and that consistency is worth more to a programme office than the extra floor area could ever be.
20x12.imageAlt: Wide exterior view of the prefabricated office cabin, 20 x 12 ft, module lines running vertically through the wall face on the 12 ft end wall.

30x10.h2: 30x10 ft, office plus store, repeated per site
30x10.intro: The office-and-store split that most sites eventually improvise, fabricated identically for every location from the start: front section working, rear third partitioned and lockable. Instrument contractors and testing agencies who must secure equipment at each posting order it as their standard site unit. Because the partition sits on the same line in every unit, the security arrangement, the racking and even the key register work identically across the whole contract footprint, from the first posting to the last.
30x10.imageAlt: Overall view of the prefabricated office cabin, 30 x 10 ft, module lines running vertically through the wall face down the 30 ft side.

40x8.h2: 40x8 ft, the linear unit for linear projects
40x8.intro: Road, rail and transmission projects live along lines, and their offices follow: a forty-foot slim body repeated at each work front, fabricated in a batch and delivered as the alignment advances. The shape fits the leftover land that linear projects actually have, and batch fabrication holds the specification steady across every chainage. Contractors order the set at award and schedule deliveries against mobilisation, so each new front opens with its office already committed, priced and on the schedule.
40x8.imageAlt: Long exterior view of the prefabricated office cabin, 40 x 8 ft, bolted panel modules meeting on a visible grid along the full 40 ft run.

40x10.h2: 40x10 ft, the package headquarters, one per package
40x10.intro: Large programmes split into packages, and each package office is this: four hundred square feet of departmentalised floor, identical at every package so reporting, filing and even furniture orders repeat cleanly. Buying them as a set at award locks the price for later packages and removes the specification drift that creeps in when each package buys its own. Programme directors who have consolidated five mismatched offices into one standard remember exactly why this page exists and order accordingly at the next award.
40x10.imageAlt: Side-on view of the prefabricated office cabin, 40 x 10 ft, module lines running vertically through the wall face across the 40 ft elevation.

20x20.h2: 20x20 ft, the square training unit, deployed in sets
20x20.intro: Induction has to happen at every site of a large contract, and the square floor is the induction room: open, central, seating in rows or clusters. Ordered as a set, every location trains in the same room with the same layout, which safety teams value because the induction itself becomes standard. The two-piece build travels like the smaller units, so even the remotest sites of the contract are not excluded from it. One drawing approval covers the entire training estate for the full life of the programme.
20x20.imageAlt: Full-length view of the prefabricated office cabin, 20 x 20 ft, bolted panel modules meeting on a visible grid around the 20 ft square plan.

40x12.h2: 40x12 ft, the flagship unit of a standardised fleet
40x12.intro: The largest unit in a standardised order: the regional or lead-site office that anchors a fleet of smaller identical cabins. Fabricated on the same batch drawing discipline, it shares its surfaces, its openings and its electrical logic with every junior unit in the order, so the fleet reads as one estate rather than a collection. Contractors running a hub-and-spoke site structure order one of these with each cluster of smaller units, and the tier pricing counts the whole mixed order as one quantity for the discount.
40x12.imageAlt: Full elevation of the prefabricated office cabin, 40 x 12 ft, bolted panel modules meeting on a visible grid over the 40 by 12 ft body.

portable-office-container.h2: Portable Office Container sizes built for relocation
portable-office-container.guidanceLine: Every unit carries reinforced lifting points and protected services as standard.

10x10.h2: 10x10 ft, the unit that moves with the work
10x10.intro: A gate office that follows the project: reinforced corner lifting points, services routed in protected conduit, and a frame stiffened for repeated craning. Event operators and short-phase contractors shift this compact unit several times in a season, and the hardening is what lets them do it without a repair bill after every move. Where an ordinary cabin is placed once and left, this one is designed around the assumption that the truck is coming back for it, this season and the next and the one after.
10x10.imageAlt: Portable office container, 10 x 10 ft, pale blue upper panel over a dark grey base, two windows and a central door seen from the corner.

20x8.h2: 20x8 ft, the slim mover for tight repeated drops
20x8.intro: The narrow body that goes where the next placement is tighter than the last: reinforced for lifting, slim enough for urban lanes, services sealed against the knocks of transit. Utility contractors moving crews between road openings keep one permanently on the truck rotation, dropping it fresh at each new stretch of road. The protected wiring loom means the office is live within an hour of touching down, and just as quickly disconnected when the stretch is done, the crew moves on and the next opening is already waiting.
20x8.imageAlt: Complete exterior of the portable office container, 20 x 8 ft, a strengthened base frame sized for repeated craning along the 20 ft flank.

20x10.h2: 20x10 ft, the standard office, hardened to travel
20x10.intro: The familiar two-hundred-square-foot office rebuilt around movement: lifting interfaces engineered to the unit's completed weight, glazing protected for transit, services terminating in a single armoured connection point. Contractors whose projects run in phases across a region relocate it between sites instead of buying twice. Each move costs transport and a crane, not refurbishment, which changes the arithmetic of owning one office across many postings entirely, which is the calculation this whole line is built on.
20x10.imageAlt: Portable office container, 20 x 10 ft, white upper panel over a charcoal base with four windows along the twenty foot flank.

20x12.h2: 20x12 ft, moving width without moving damage
20x12.intro: The wider floor with the meeting corner, built to survive the journey between placements: stiffened top frame, protected service runs, lifting points matched to the extra width. Project teams that host client reviews and then move on take it because the meeting room travels along with the project instead of being rebuilt from nothing each phase. What normally suffers in a relocated cabin is the fit-out, and here the fit-out is anchored and shielded from the outset, specifically because relocation is the plan.
20x12.imageAlt: Wide exterior view of the portable office container, 20 x 12 ft, a strengthened base frame sized for repeated craning on the 12 ft end wall.

30x10.h2: 30x10 ft, office and store that redeploy together
30x10.intro: The partitioned office-plus-store as a single relocatable body: instruments stay in their lockable rear room during the move, and the whole unit lifts as one sealed piece. Survey and geotechnical teams working campaign-style across sites redeploy it with the equipment still racked and locked inside, saving a full pack-up and set-down at every single move. The stiffened frame is what makes travelling loaded acceptable, and that capability is the whole difference between this and simply partitioning an ordinary cabin.
30x10.imageAlt: Overall view of the portable office container, 30 x 10 ft, a strengthened base frame sized for repeated craning down the 30 ft side.

40x8.h2: 40x8 ft, the long unit that follows the alignment
40x8.intro: Linear projects advance, and this office advances with them: a forty-foot slim body lifted from chainage to chainage as fronts complete. The length demands proper lifting engineering, and that is precisely what the hardened frame and matched lift points provide. Road and pipeline contractors move it three or four times across a package instead of placing a new cabin at each front, and the protected loom re-terminates at each drop without an electrician rebuilding the connection from scratch at every single drop.
40x8.imageAlt: Long exterior view of the portable office container, 40 x 8 ft, reinforced lifting points built into each corner along the full 40 ft run.

40x10.h2: 40x10 ft, headquarters that transfer between projects
40x10.intro: A full four-hundred-square-foot project office engineered to serve consecutive projects rather than one: transferred by crane and trailer at each demobilisation, arriving at the next award with its zones, services and fittings intact. Contractors treat it as plant, moving it project to project on the asset register, and the hardening is what preserves its value across those transfers. The alternative is buying a headquarters at every award and abandoning that embedded value at every project close-out.
40x10.imageAlt: Side-on view of the portable office container, 40 x 10 ft, a strengthened base frame sized for repeated craning across the 40 ft elevation.

20x20.h2: 20x20 ft, the square that splits, moves and rejoins
20x20.intro: The two-piece square with relocation designed into the joint: each half lifts separately on its own reinforced points, travels as a standard load, and rejoins with the sealed floor strip and paired electrical sets re-mating at the new site. Training rooms and control rooms that must exist at each phase of a long programme move this way. Rejoining is a procedure, not an improvisation, because the joint was engineered for its fifth mating, and not merely its first, which is where improvised joints fail.
20x20.imageAlt: Full-length view of the portable office container, 20 x 20 ft, reinforced lifting points built into each corner around the 20 ft square plan.

40x12.h2: 40x12 ft, the largest office we build to move
40x12.intro: Four hundred and eighty square feet engineered for a life of placements: the heaviest unit in this line, and therefore the one where lifting-point engineering and frame stiffening matter most. Organisations running long rotations, mine services, large EPC houses, plant hire, keep one or two circulating between commitments. It is the most office that can follow the work as a single body, and the hardening premium is what keeps it working after the fifth site instead of giving up somewhere around the second.
40x12.imageAlt: Full elevation of the portable office container, 40 x 12 ft, reinforced lifting points built into each corner over the 40 by 12 ft body.

small-office-cabin.h2: Small Office Cabin sizes for one to four people
small-office-cabin.guidanceLine: Three compact sizes only. Larger floors live on our main office range page.

10x10.h2: 10x10 ft, the two-person office in its element
10x10.intro: One hundred square feet arranged for two people who share a task: a security supervisor beside the CCTV desk, a cashier with the records, a doctor with an assistant. This page's whole purpose is the compact brief, so the smallest size is its centre of gravity rather than its afterthought. The cabin lands, connects and works the same day, and the nine-foot ceiling keeps a small footprint from feeling like a box. Most buyers here never needed anything larger, and nothing larger is ever pushed at them here.
10x10.imageAlt: Full side view of the small office cabin, 10 x 10 ft, a single-bay body with one door and one window across the 10 ft wall.

20x8.h2: 20x8 ft, three desks where depth does not exist
20x8.intro: The compact answer for narrow ground: three desks in a row against the long wall, a door at the end, and a footprint that slots beside a gate, along a boundary or behind a showroom. Small teams that outgrew a guard-post-sized room but have no depth to spare step up to this shape and stop there. It shares the slim body of the bigger ranges but is bought here for a different reason: not because the plot is a corridor, but because the team is three people and perfectly honest with itself about staying that way.
20x8.imageAlt: Complete exterior of the small office cabin, 20 x 8 ft, a compact body proportioned for a tight site corner along the 20 ft flank.

20x10.h2: 20x10 ft, the largest office this page will sell you
20x10.intro: Two hundred square feet for four people, and deliberately the ceiling of this range: anything bigger belongs on the main range page with the full nine-size ladder. Kept here because a four-person office is still a small office, and the buyer comparing it with the two smaller sizes is making a compact-office decision, not a site-headquarters decision dressed up small. The fit-out matches the smaller sizes exactly, so growing from the 10x10 to this floor changes the floor area and changes nothing else at all.
20x10.imageAlt: The whole small office cabin, 20 x 10 ft, a single-bay body with one door and one window over the 20 ft length.

labor-colony.h2: Every labour colony size, and the site each one runs

60x24-gplus1.h2: 60x24 ft G+1, 2880 sq ft planned for 58 to 72 workers
60x24-gplus1.intro: The smallest colony dormitory holds 58 to 72 workers over two floors and usually anchors a compact site with one toilet block beside it. At 2,880 square feet it fits plots where a longer building will not, and the flat colony rate of Rs 675 per square foot keeps its cost at Rs 19,44,000 ex-GST. Phased sites place it first and let later blocks join the planned services spine. Ask for the colony starter plan and the quotation includes the matching toilet block position on your plot. Site lighting on the access side is part of the standard scope.
60x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour colony, 60x24 ft G+1, from the front left with the end stair, two floors on a 60 ft footprint in the multi-block housing build.

90x24-gplus1.h2: 90x24 ft G+1, 4320 sq ft planned for 86 to 108 workers
90x24-gplus1.intro: Ninety feet of building over two floors sleeps 86 to 108 workers, which matches the crew of a mid-size civil package. This is the configuration our own costing sheet uses as its reference for the whole cluster, so quotations on it turn around fastest. The dormitory pairs with a four-seat toilet block on the standard site plan, and the 4,320 square feet price out at Rs 29,16,000 ex-GST with nothing added for size. Because it is the costing reference, its drawings are the most exercised in the library and surprises are rare. Its toilet-block pairing is drawn at four stalls per floor.
90x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour colony, 90x24 ft G+1, from the left corner at the stair end, two floors on a 90 ft footprint in the multi-block housing build.

90x24-gplus2.h2: 90x24 ft G+2, 6480 sq ft planned for 129 to 162 workers
90x24-gplus2.intro: Adding a third floor to the 90 ft footprint lifts capacity to 129 to 162 workers without taking one extra foot of plot, which is why tight urban sites choose it. Stair towers at the building end serve all three levels, and the structure is engineered for the extra storey from the base up rather than adapted later. The 6,480 square feet list at Rs 43,74,000 ex-GST at the same flat rate every other size uses. Local height clearances are the one item to confirm early, and our drawing pack includes what approvers ask for.
90x24-gplus2.imageAlt: Labour colony, 90x24 ft G+2, from the stair end on the left, three floors on a 90 ft footprint in the multi-block housing build.

120x24-gplus1.h2: 120x24 ft G+1, 5760 sq ft planned for 115 to 144 workers
120x24-gplus1.intro: The 120 ft two-floor building is the workhorse of large colonies: 115 to 144 workers in one block, long straight rooms that furnish quickly, and a footprint that packs efficiently in rows with fire separation between them. Most multi-building colonies are laid out as repeats of this unit. Its 5,760 square feet total Rs 38,88,000 ex-GST, the figure the hub record carries. Row spacing and fire separation dimensions for repeat layouts ship with the first quotation as standard. Gate distance and muster areas are marked on the same layout sheet.
120x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour colony, 120x24 ft G+1, from the front left with the end stair, two floors on a 120 ft footprint in the multi-block housing build.

118x30-gplus1.h2: 118x30 ft G+1, 7080 sq ft planned for 142 to 177 workers
118x30-gplus1.intro: The 30 ft wide body changes the internal planning: deeper rooms, wider aisles and space for in-block amenities that the 24 ft buildings push to separate blocks. With 142 to 177 workers over two floors and 7,080 square feet, it suits employers who want fewer, better buildings rather than more repeats. Cost follows the same rule as every size, Rs 47,79,000 ex-GST. Employers housing supervisors alongside crews usually reserve the wide body's deeper rooms for that purpose. Verandah options along the long face are quoted on request.
118x30-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour colony, 118x30 ft G+1, from the left corner at the stair end, two floors on the wide 30 ft body in the multi-block housing build.

120x24-gplus2.h2: 120x24 ft G+2, 8640 sq ft planned for 173 to 216 workers
120x24-gplus2.intro: Three floors on the 120 ft footprint make the largest single dormitory we build: 173 to 216 workers, 8,640 square feet, one stair core serving all levels. A pair of these houses a four-hundred-strong workforce on remarkably little land. It prices at Rs 58,32,000 ex-GST, and like every configuration on this page that figure is area times the flat colony rate, nothing else. Where two of these stand together the services spine between them is designed once and shared by both. Water storage for all floors sits on the stair-core roof slab.
120x24-gplus2.imageAlt: Labour colony, 120x24 ft G+2, from the stair end on the left, three floors on a 120 ft footprint in the multi-block housing build.

20x10.h2: 20x10 ft Labour Shed: 200 sq ft With a Single Bunk Row
20x10.intro: The smallest published shed. At 10 ft wide there is room for one bunk row along a single long wall and a clear walking aisle beside it, so the plan stays simple and the exit is never blocked by a bed. It suits a small gang, a night shift crew or a remote outpost where a full hall is not justified. Below this footprint a shed stops making sense: the frame, roof and door cost much the same whatever the length, so an insulated PUF porta cabin becomes the better buy.
20x10.imageAlt: 20x10 ft labour shed exterior shown as the 200 sq ft size option in the selector

20x15.h2: 20x15 ft Labour Shed: 300 sq ft, Two Rows and Aisle
20x15.intro: Fifteen feet of width is the point where a second bunk row becomes practical. Bunks sit against both long walls with a central aisle between them, which roughly doubles the beds without doubling the roof or the slab. This is the first size that behaves like a proper dormitory rather than a bunk room, and it is a common choice for a single trade gang working one defined package on a short site programme.
20x15.imageAlt: 20x15 ft labour shed exterior shown as the 300 sq ft size option in the selector

20x20.h2: 20x20 ft Labour Shed: 400 sq ft With a Wider Centre Aisle
20x20.intro: At 20 ft square the hall becomes genuinely comfortable to move through. The extra width goes into the central aisle and into locker space at each end, so men can dress and store kit without standing on each other at shift change. Cleaning is faster too, because the aisle takes a trolley rather than forcing hand work between beds. Choose this when occupancy is steady and the shed will stand for several months.
20x20.imageAlt: 20x20 ft labour shed exterior shown as the 400 sq ft size option in the selector

20x25.h2: 20x25 ft Labour Shed: 500 sq ft, Mid-Point Second Exit
20x25.intro: Length is what changes here rather than width. At 25 ft the walk from the far bunk to a single door gets long, so a second personnel door goes into the long wall near the mid-point. Two exits shorten travel distance in an emergency and give the hall a second cross-flow air path on still days. This is the size at which exit planning starts to drive the hall layout rather than simply follow it.
20x25.imageAlt: 20x25 ft labour shed exterior shown as the 500 sq ft size option in the selector

20x30.h2: 20x30 ft Labour Shed: 600 sq ft With a Door at Each End
20x30.intro: Thirty feet gives a full-length central aisle running door to door, which is the cleanest circulation this product achieves. Air enters through the louvre band along both walls, crosses the bunks and leaves at the ridge without anything blocking the path. It is the size we use as the reference plan on the technical drawing, because at 30 ft every control the shed depends on is visible in a single view.
20x30.imageAlt: 20x30 ft labour shed exterior shown as the 600 sq ft reference size option in the selector

20x40.h2: 20x40 ft Labour Shed: 800 sq ft, Three Distributed Exits
20x40.intro: The largest published shed and the lowest rate per square foot, because one roof and one slab now cover twice the floor of the 20x20. Two long bunk rows face a full-length aisle, with three doors distributed along the length so no bunk sits far from an exit. Beyond this footprint the frame needs a wider clear span, so the shed is engineered and quoted individually rather than taken from the published six.
20x40.imageAlt: 20x40 ft labour shed exterior shown as the 800 sq ft size option in the selector

labor-hutments.h2: Every labour hutment size, and the rooms each block gives

60x24-gplus1.h2: 60x24 ft G+1, 2880 sq ft planned for 58 to 72 workers
60x24-gplus1.intro: The small hutment gives two floors of individual rooms for 58 to 72 workers, each room with its own door, window, fan and board. Short passages serve a handful of rooms per floor, so gangs keep to their own space and belongings stay behind a lock. It is the configuration for smaller mixed crews, and its 2,880 square feet come in at Rs 19,82,880 ex-GST. Couples employed together on site are usually allocated the end rooms, which sit apart from the gang rooms. Every room lock is master-keyed for the site office.
60x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour hutment, 60x24 ft G+1, from the front left with the end stair, two floors on a 60 ft footprint in the room-block hutment build.

90x24-gplus1.h2: 90x24 ft G+1, 4320 sq ft planned for 86 to 108 workers
90x24-gplus1.intro: Ninety feet of rooms over two floors houses 86 to 108 workers in the best-balanced room block we make. The passage runs the building's length with rooms off one side, so every door is visible without entering any room. Supervisors and chargehands usually take the end rooms. At the hutment rate of Rs 688.50 per square foot, 4,320 square feet amount to Rs 29,74,320 ex-GST. Its room count divides cleanly by common gang sizes, which is why allocation plans on it stay tidy. Passage lighting runs on its own night circuit.
90x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour hutment, 90x24 ft G+1, from the left corner at the stair end, two floors on a 90 ft footprint in the room-block hutment build.

90x24-gplus2.h2: 90x24 ft G+2, 6480 sq ft planned for 129 to 162 workers
90x24-gplus2.intro: Three floors of rooms on the 90 ft plinth reach 129 to 162 workers while the plot stays the size of the two-floor block. Rooms repeat identically on every level, which simplifies allocation by gang and by shift, and the stair discipline is easier with rooms than with halls. The 6,480 square feet land at Rs 44,61,480 ex-GST. Water points and washing lines stay at ground level on the standard plan, so upper floors remain purely sleeping space and the plinth drains stay simple. The stair tower includes the luggage winch point that three-floor room blocks need on moving day.
90x24-gplus2.imageAlt: Labour hutment, 90x24 ft G+2, from the stair end on the left, three floors on a 90 ft footprint in the room-block hutment build.

120x24-gplus1.h2: 120x24 ft G+1, 5760 sq ft planned for 115 to 144 workers
120x24-gplus1.intro: The 120 ft room block sleeps 115 to 144 workers and suits long postings where crews live on site for seasons rather than weeks. More rooms per floor means finer-grained allocation: gangs, trades and shifts each get their own doors. Its 5,760 square feet work out at Rs 39,65,760 ex-GST, calculated exactly like every other size here. Each room keeps the standard fit of bunks, fan, board and window, so moving a gang between blocks never means re-briefing anyone on the accommodation. Season after season the same room keys go to the same gangs, and that continuity shows in how the block is kept.
120x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour hutment, 120x24 ft G+1, from the front left with the end stair, two floors on a 120 ft footprint in the room-block hutment build.

118x30-gplus1.h2: 118x30 ft G+1, 7080 sq ft planned for 142 to 177 workers
118x30-gplus1.intro: With a 30 ft body the rooms deepen enough for four-bunk layouts, taking 142 to 177 workers while keeping the lockable-room principle. The wide block is chosen when employers upgrade housing standards without moving to family accommodation. Price for the 7,080 square feet is Rs 48,74,580 ex-GST. The deeper rooms also take a table and stools between the bunk rows, which crews on long postings ask for more than any other single feature in this range. The four-bunk rooms also meet client-audit standards that some principal contractors now write into subcontracts.
118x30-gplus1.imageAlt: Labour hutment, 118x30 ft G+1, from the left corner at the stair end, two floors on the wide 30 ft body in the room-block hutment build.

120x24-gplus2.h2: 120x24 ft G+2, 8640 sq ft planned for 173 to 216 workers
120x24-gplus2.intro: The largest hutment stacks three floors of rooms on the 120 ft footprint for a 173 to 216 worker strength, the deepest private-room capacity in the cluster. One stair core and repeated room modules keep it simple to run despite its size. At the flat hutment rate its 8,640 square feet run to Rs 59,48,640 ex-GST. Room allocation by floor keeps day and night shifts apart without a supervisor standing at the stair, and the top floor is usually held for chargehands. Its scale justifies a dedicated caretaker room beside the stair, which the standard plan already reserves.
120x24-gplus2.imageAlt: Labour hutment, 120x24 ft G+2, from the stair end on the left, three floors on a 120 ft footprint in the room-block hutment build.

prefab-labor-camps.h2: Every prefab labour camp size, and the move each one makes

60x24-gplus1.h2: 60x24 ft G+1, 2880 sq ft planned for 58 to 72 workers
60x24-gplus1.intro: The starter camp block holds 58 to 72 workers on two panel-built floors, and its whole point is the second site: bolted joints, pedestal footings and plug-in services come apart in days and go back up at the next project. Contractors who won two-year packages in different states buy this block first. Its 2,880 square feet list at Rs 19,56,960 ex-GST. The trailer count and crane hours for a move are stated on the quotation, so relocation is budgeted before purchase. Panel counts per trailer are listed in the quote.
60x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Prefab labour camp, 60x24 ft G+1, from the front left with the end stair, two floors on a 60 ft footprint in the bolted panel camp build.

90x24-gplus1.h2: 90x24 ft G+1, 4320 sq ft planned for 86 to 108 workers
90x24-gplus1.intro: The 90 ft camp block sleeps 86 to 108 workers and is the unit most often ordered in pairs, one block either side of the services spine. Panel joints repeat on a fixed module, so a damaged panel swaps rather than condemns a wall. At Rs 679.50 per square foot, its 4,320 square feet total Rs 29,35,440 ex-GST. The pair arrives as matched panel kits on separate trailers, and the second block is typically standing seven working days after the first bolt goes in. Spare panels ordered with the block travel with it between sites, insurance that has saved more than one monsoon.
90x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Prefab labour camp, 90x24 ft G+1, from the left corner at the stair end, two floors on a 90 ft footprint in the bolted panel camp build.

90x24-gplus2.h2: 90x24 ft G+2, 6480 sq ft planned for 129 to 162 workers
90x24-gplus2.intro: Three panel floors on the 90 ft footprint carry 129 to 162 workers and still dismantle: the third storey bolts to the same module as the first, and the stair tower unbolts into liftable sections. Sites that relocate but cannot spread outward order this one. The 6,480 square feet come in at Rs 44,03,160 ex-GST. Nothing about the third floor is special order; it is the same wall, floor and roof panels from the same module library, which is what keeps relocation honest. Dismantling simply reverses assembly, numbered panels back onto their trailers. Pad positions are pre-marked on the ground template.
90x24-gplus2.imageAlt: Prefab labour camp, 90x24 ft G+2, from the stair end on the left, three floors on a 90 ft footprint in the bolted panel camp build.

120x24-gplus1.h2: 120x24 ft G+1, 5760 sq ft planned for 115 to 144 workers
120x24-gplus1.intro: At 120 ft over two floors the camp reaches 115 to 144 workers, the standard block for big relocatable sites. External cable trays and quick-connect water runs mean hookup at a new site takes a crew days, not weeks. Its 5,760 square feet amount to Rs 39,13,920 ex-GST on the same flat basis as the rest of the ladder. Foundations are pedestal pads rather than a slab, so leaving a site means lifting pads, not breaking concrete, and the ground reinstates in days. Hookup drawings are issued per site, and repeat customers keep the same block numbering across every project.
120x24-gplus1.imageAlt: Prefab labour camp, 120x24 ft G+1, from the front left with the end stair, two floors on a 120 ft footprint in the bolted panel camp build.

118x30-gplus1.h2: 118x30 ft G+1, 7080 sq ft planned for 142 to 177 workers
118x30-gplus1.intro: The wide 30 ft camp body earns its width at the services spine: deeper rooms on one side, a full-width utility zone on the other, all still bolted and movable. It houses 142 to 177 workers across two floors. The 7,080 square feet land at Rs 48,10,860 ex-GST. Its width suits camps that centralise cooking and washing in the block itself rather than in separate service buildings, keeping the site footprint tight. The utility zone takes water heaters and treatment units indoors, which matters in cold-region postings.
118x30-gplus1.imageAlt: Prefab labour camp, 118x30 ft G+1, from the left corner at the stair end, two floors on the wide 30 ft body in the bolted panel camp build.

120x24-gplus2.h2: 120x24 ft G+2, 8640 sq ft planned for 173 to 216 workers
120x24-gplus2.intro: The largest camp stacks three 120 ft panel floors for 173 to 216 workers and remains fully demountable, which no other building this size in the cluster offers. Where a mega-project ends and another begins, this block moves whole. Its 8,640 square feet work out at Rs 58,70,880 ex-GST. When it finally stops moving, the same block converts to a permanent installation by grouting the pedestals, with no structural change above the base. Owners who repeat this block across projects report the second erection takes half the hours of the first. A move log ships with the block's document set.
120x24-gplus2.imageAlt: Prefab labour camp, 120x24 ft G+2, from the stair end on the left, three floors on a 120 ft footprint in the bolted panel camp build.

20x8.h2: 20x8 ft Converted Container for a Small Resident Crew
20x8.intro: This is the smallest unit we build, and it starts life as a used 20 ft shipping container. We strip the donor shell, repair corrosion, cut and reinforce the openings, then insulate and line it. At 8 ft internal width the plan runs one bunk line down one side with a walking aisle beside it. Site managers choose it for a gate crew, a security detail or a supervisor pair, and for sites where the crane window is short and the unit must land in one lift.

20x10.h2: 20x10 ft Wide-Body Sleeping Module on a Short Footprint
20x10.intro: At 10 ft width the plan changes completely. Two bunk runs face each other across a central aisle, so the same length holds a materially larger crew and people can pass without turning sideways. No shipping container is made 10 ft wide, so we fabricate this one from MS corrugated sheet on a new steel frame. It is the reference size for our specification and the one most sites start with when the footprint is tight but the headcount is not.

30x10.h2: 30x10 ft Wide-Body Module for a Camp That Stays Put
30x10.intro: Thirty feet gives you room the 20 ft sizes cannot: a locker and storage zone at one end without stealing bunk space, and enough wall to place windows for genuine cross-ventilation. Fabricated wide-body, like every 10 ft unit. Choose it when the camp is settled for a season or more and the crew needs somewhere to keep kit dry. It also transports on a standard trailer, which the 40 ft sizes do not always do on a constrained access road.

40x8.h2: 40x8 ft Converted Container on a Standard ISO Footprint
40x8.intro: The second conversion size, built on a used 40 ft shipping container. You get double the length of the 20x8 at the same 8 ft width, so the plan stays a single bunk run with a side aisle and simply runs longer. It suits sites that already handle 40 ft units and have the yard equipment and access for them. Because the donor shell is second-hand, we inspect and record its condition before quoting, and structural repair is priced against what we find.

40x10.h2: 40x10 ft Wide-Body Module for a Full Night Shift Crew
40x10.intro: This is the workhorse of the range. Forty feet of length at 10 ft width gives two long bunk runs, a central aisle that stays walkable when everyone is changing at once, and enough wall for a proper window and fan layout. Fabricated wide-body. Most sites reach it when one shift no longer fits a 30 ft unit and splitting the crew across two smaller modules costs more in transport than one larger one.

40x12.h2: 40x12 ft Wide-Body Module with the Widest Central Aisle
40x12.intro: The widest unit we build, and the only one where the central aisle stops being a corridor. Twelve feet leaves room for lockers along the aisle without narrowing it, which matters when a crew changes shift together rather than in ones and twos. Fabricated wide-body on a new steel frame. Check your transport route first: at 12 ft the unit is an over-dimension load on most Indian roads and needs the permit and escort arranged before dispatch.
